name: Epristeride

lead: Epristeride is an oral 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that people in hair-loss communities discuss as a finasteride-like way to hold on to scalp hair. It is sold in China for enlarged prostate.

It blocks the type 2 form of the enzyme that turns testosterone into DHT, the hormone linked to follicle miniaturisation and pattern hair loss. Less DHT means less thinning over time. Hair loss and acne were explored as uses during development but were never approved, and no published hair-loss trial results turned up.

paras: People who use it treat it as an alternative to finasteride, taken by mouth as a daily tablet, usually alongside other hair-loss measures. Hair-loss drugs of this type are generally kept up long term, with results judged over many months.
Safety information is sparse. As a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor it is prescription-only where it is marketed, and it is not sold in the US, UK or Japan.

angle.text: Epristeride lowers DHT, the hormone that shrinks scalp follicles, so the goal is slower thinning and more hair kept. Hair-loss forum users discuss it as a finasteride-like option. It is marketed in China for prostate enlargement, and its hair use was explored but never approved.

lead: Epristeride is an oral steroidal 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that lowers conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). It is marketed in China for benign prostatic hyperplasia under brand names including Aipuliete and Chuanliu.[1]

For hair, the relevant chain is DHT. Pattern hair loss involves follicles that shrink under DHT signalling, so a drug that lowers DHT is a candidate for slowing that process. Epristeride is discussed in hair-loss circles as a lesser-known relative of finasteride, but the hair-loss indication was explored during development and never approved.[1]

DHT drives miniaturisation of scalp hair follicles in male pattern hair loss, which is why 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride and dutasteride are used to keep and thicken hair. Epristeride works on the same enzyme by a different, uncompetitive mechanism, so it appears in hair-loss discussion as a finasteride-like compound.[2] It was investigated for male pattern hair loss and acne during development, but those uses were never approved, according to Wikipedia.[1]

Research on epristeride is mainly in prostate disease: a 141-patient Chinese study, a 906-patient randomised comparison of seven BPH drug groups that included epristeride, pharmacokinetic work in healthy men, and laboratory studies.[3][4][5] No hair-loss trial results were found.
infobox: Prescription only (China); not marketed in US, UK, Japan

paras: Epristeride is a synthetic androstane steroid, chemically 17beta-(tert-butylcarbamoyl)androsta-3,5-diene-3-carboxylic acid, with a molar mass of about 399.6 g/mol. Wikipedia reports that it can be synthesised starting from progesterone.[1] It is a prescription product in China, where it is sold as Aipuliete and Chuanliu.[1]
Like finasteride it is selective for type 2 5-alpha-reductase, unlike dutasteride, and it works by an uncompetitive mechanism instead of finasteride's competitive binding.[1][2][6]

Epristeride is used in China for benign prostatic hyperplasia.[1] Wikipedia states that it was studied for androgenic alopecia and acne without receiving approval for either.[1] A 1998 pipeline report described it as under development by SmithKline Beecham for BPH and acne.[7]

It inhibits the type 2 isoform of 5-alpha-reductase through an uncompetitive mechanism, forming a complex with the enzyme, testosterone and NADPH.[1][2] A 1994 study characterised it as selective and specific for human isoform 2, noting that specificity has implications for a compound's therapeutic potential and safety.[2] Comparative tissue work examined its sensitivity alongside finasteride in prostate and skin tissue.[8] Finasteride is competitive and epristeride non-competitive, and a hybrid of the two was designed in 2011 as a new inhibitor.[6] Wikipedia reports that epristeride lowers circulating DHT by about 25 to 54 percent despite high in-vitro potency.[1] In healthy male volunteers it reduced serum DHT while serum testosterone stayed stable, and animal work showed potency similar to finasteride.[7]

In cell culture, epristeride dose-dependently inhibited testosterone-induced growth of stromal cells from hyperplastic prostates but did not affect DHT-induced growth.[9] Rat studies reported changes in TGF-beta receptor expression in prostate cells and IGF-1 and TGF-beta receptor expression in castrated rat prostate,[10][11] and a beagle study compared competitive and non-competitive inhibitors on serum and intra-prostatic androgens.[12]

Wikipedia describes epristeride as very potent against the type 2 enzyme in vitro (roughly 0.18 to 2 nM) yet lowering circulating DHT by about 25 to 54 percent after eight days across a wide range of doses, a reduction the article states is smaller than that of finasteride or dutasteride.[1] It adds that early expectations that intraprostatic testosterone would not rise with epristeride, unlike with finasteride and dutasteride, were not supported by later clinical data.[1]

In a crossover study of 12 healthy men aged about 27, each received a single 5 mg oral dose and a 4.5 mg intravenous infusion, with plasma sampled over 72 hours, to determine absolute bioavailability.[5] Wikipedia gives oral bioavailability of about 93 percent and an elimination half-life of about 26 hours.[1]
No studies found for hair loss.

In BPH, a Chinese study gave 141 patients aged 50 to 83 epristeride 5 mg twice daily for 120 days and reported a total efficacy of 81.29 percent on symptom score, flow rate, prostate volume and residual urine. Adverse reactions included erectile dysfunction in 3 patients (2.16 percent) and single cases of rash, nausea and vomiting, insomnia and tinnitus; two patients stopped treatment because of side effects.[3] A randomised, parallel-controlled, multicentre trial from September 2002 to December 2003 enrolled 906 BPH patients into seven groups, including alpha-blockers, the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors finasteride and epristeride, and the plant product cernilton.[4] Wikipedia mentions that it reached phase III trials for BPH, androgenic alopecia and acne in the US, UK and Japan without being marketed there.[1]

In the 141-patient Chinese BPH study, reactions were uncommon: erectile dysfunction in 2.16 percent, and rash, nausea and vomiting, insomnia and tinnitus in one patient each.[3] A rat study examining androgen depletion with epristeride, bicalutamide and a lyase inhibitor reported effects on chemically induced prostate carcinogenesis.[13] Wider safety data for hair-loss use are not available.

SmithKline Beecham developed epristeride in the 1990s for BPH, androgenic alopecia and acne. It was not marketed in the US, UK or Japan. Ono Pharmaceutical developed and introduced it for BPH in China in 2000.[1] The 1998 pipeline report described it as a transition-state, noncompetitive steroid inhibitor with phase III prostate trials initiated in the UK, US and Japan; it was licensed to Ono for Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, and Recordati held co-marketing rights.[7]

Wikipedia states that SmithKline Beecham, now part of GlaxoSmithKline, developed the drug in the 1990s for BPH, androgenic alopecia and acne, that it reached phase III trials in the US, UK and Japan without being marketed there, and that Ono Pharmaceutical introduced it in China in 2000.[1]

Epristeride is sold only in China according to Wikipedia, as a prescription medicine for prostate enlargement.[1] In hair-loss discussion it appears mainly as a comparison point for finasteride and dutasteride, since published human data concern the prostate rather than scalp hair.[3][4] No clinical hair-loss trial of epristeride has been published, and it is not an approved hair-loss product anywhere.
